notes: Ruling slot 1 = Busia's Progress Party (Second Republic, elected Aug 1969). Template coalition slot 2 holds Gbedemah's National Alliance of Liberals, which is actually the official opposition, not a coalition partner. CPP stays in slot 4 as in MD (banned since 1966). Slot 13 = the Presidential Commission (Afrifa, Ocran, Harlley) acting as head of state on 1 Jan 1970. MD anachronisms (NPP, NDC, PNC, EGLE, DPP, NDP, PPP) replaced.

0.name: Operation Cold Chop
0.text:
Operation Cold Chop was the codename of the coup of 24 February 1966 that overthrew Kwame Nkrumah. The officers and police commanders who planned it, among them Akwasi Afrifa and the police chief John Harlley, remain a tight network with friends in Washington and London even after handing power to civilians in 1969.

They see themselves as guardians against a return of Nkrumahism, favour firm security laws, a pro-Western foreign policy and economic discipline, and distrust politicians who stray from that course. Their base is the officer corps and the police Special Branch. Their leverage is simple: they have removed a government once before.

1.name: Progress Party
1.text:
The Progress Party was founded in 1969 by heirs of the Danquah-Busia tradition and won 105 of 140 seats in the August elections. On 1 January 1970 it governs the Second Republic under Prime Minister Kofi Abrefa Busia, the Oxford-trained sociologist who led the opposition to Nkrumah from exile.

The party stands for parliamentary democracy, private enterprise, rural development and close ties to Britain and the United States, and it has begun expelling undocumented aliens and rolling back Nkrumah's state enterprises. Its base is the Akan heartland, Ashanti and Brong-Ahafo, the professions and cocoa farmers. Its leverage lies in its large majority and the backing of the chiefs.

2.name: National Alliance of Liberals
2.text:
The National Alliance of Liberals was formed in 1969 by Komla Agbeli Gbedemah, Nkrumah's former finance minister who broke with him in 1961. It won 29 seats and forms the official opposition, but Gbedemah's own seat is contested under constitutional rules barring officials found guilty of misconduct by the asset commissions.

The NAL accepts the market economy and Western partnership but defends civil liberties, a fairer share for the Volta Region and a gentler line on former CPP members. Its base is the Ewe of the Volta Region and moderate ex-Nkrumahists in Accra. Its leverage lies in its role as the main parliamentary alternative.

3.name: Ghana Trades Union Congress
3.text:
The Ghana TUC, an arm of the CPP under Nkrumah, was rebuilt after 1966 as an independent labour centre. Under its secretary-general Benjamin Bentum it has become increasingly critical of the Busia government's austerity and of laws that restrict strikes.

The TUC demands wage rises to match inflation, protection of public-sector jobs and a voice in economic policy, while rejecting a return to party control of the unions. Its members are miners, dockworkers, railwaymen and civil servants. Its leverage lies in strikes in Takoradi, Tema and the gold mines, which can paralyse the export economy.

4.name: Convention People's Party
4.text:
The Convention People's Party led the Gold Coast to independence in 1957 and became Ghana's sole legal party in 1964. Banned after the 1966 coup, it has no legal existence on 1 January 1970. Kwame Nkrumah lives in exile in Conakry as honorary co-president of Guinea, broadcasting appeals to his followers.

The CPP's loyalists want Nkrumah's return, scientific socialism, state industry, a united Africa and close ties to the Soviet bloc and China. Its base is urban workers, former party officials and youth who remember the independence years. Its leverage lies in Nkrumah's lasting prestige and in disappointment with austerity.

5.name: Spark Group
5.text:
The Spark was the Marxist weekly of Nkrumah's ideological wing, edited by Kofi Batsa and read across radical Africa. Its writers were detained after the 1966 coup and the paper closed, but its circle of journalists, lecturers and former Winneba ideological instructors still meets in private.

They call for a socialist revolution beyond Nkrumah's compromises, nationalisation of the mines and banks, an end to the IMF programme and solidarity with liberation movements. Their base is young intellectuals and students in Accra and Legon. Their leverage lies in the pen and in sympathy among students frustrated by the new regime.

6.name: Verandah Boys
6.text:
The Verandah Boys were the unemployed young men who slept on verandahs and formed Nkrumah's earliest militants in 1949. The name survives for the hard nationalist rank and file of the old CPP who see the Busia government as a restoration of the old elites and Western dominance.

They are less interested in Marxist theory than in national pride, jobs and revenge for 1966. They condemn the expulsion of aliens as a Western-inspired policy, decry IMF austerity and look to Moscow and Conakry for support. Their base is the urban poor of Accra, Kumasi and Sekondi. Their leverage lies in numbers and anger.

7.name: President's Own Guard Regiment
7.text:
The President's Own Guard Regiment was Nkrumah's Soviet-trained praetorian force, built up outside the regular army and loyal to him personally. It fought briefly at Flagstaff House during the 1966 coup and was disbanded, its officers dismissed or absorbed into other units.

Its former members favour a strong one-party state, a security service on the Eastern model and alignment with the socialist camp. Their base is scattered veterans and old intelligence officials who still have contacts in Conakry and Eastern Europe. Their leverage lies in military skills and the hope of foreign support for a counter-coup.

8.name: Sons of Jabal Amil
8.text:
Accra's Lebanese merchants, many of them Shia from Jabal Amil in southern Lebanon, have run shops and import houses in Ghana since colonial times. They follow the rise of Imam Musa al-Sadr, who founded the Supreme Islamic Shia Council in 1969, and support his schools and charities.

The community favours a modern, socially engaged Shia identity, stays neutral in Ghanaian politics and fears the Busia government's campaign against aliens. Its base is traders in Accra, Kumasi and Takoradi. Its leverage lies in commerce and credit, though its legal status depends on the government's goodwill.

9.name: Ashura Mourners of Accra
9.text:
A devout minority within Accra's Lebanese Shia community gathers each Muharram to mourn Imam Husayn and follows the senior clerics of Najaf rather than the businessmen who lead the community. A few of its sons study in the Iraqi seminaries.

They favour strict religious observance, clerical guidance in community affairs and solidarity with the Shia of Lebanon and Iraq against Western and Zionist power. Their following is very small and inward-looking. Their leverage lies in religious authority within the diaspora and in its links to clerical networks in the Middle East.

10.name: Anbariyya Sunni Community
10.text:
In Tamale the scholar Afa Ajura, known as Yusuf Ajura, has built the Anbariyya movement since the 1940s, preaching a return to the Qur'an and Sunna against Sufi and customary practices. By 1970 it is the leading reformist Sunni current in northern Ghana and a rival of the Tijaniyya.

The movement teaches scriptural purity, Arabic learning and obedience to lawful authority rather than revolutionary politics. Its followers are Dagomba townsmen, traders and young scholars in the north. Its leverage lies in its schools and preaching circles and in its growing ties to Saudi and Egyptian institutions.

11.name: Zongo Mujahidin
11.text:
In the zongos, the Muslim quarters of Accra, Kumasi and Tamale, a handful of young men influenced by Hausa and Nigerian preachers dream of an Islamic state on the model of Usman dan Fodio's nineteenth-century caliphate. Busia's expulsion of Nigerian and Sahelian aliens has hardened their anger.

They reject the secular constitution, the Christian-dominated elite and both Cold War blocs, and call for sharia rule. Their following is tiny and loosely organised. Their leverage lies in the grievances of zongo communities who feel targeted as foreigners in their own country.

12.name: Ghana Muslim Mission
12.text:
The Ghana Muslim Mission was founded in 1957 to provide modern education for Muslim children and to give the community a voice in the new state. It runs schools in Kumasi and the north and works with Muslim politicians who once belonged to the Muslim Association Party.

The Mission seeks equal access to schools and public jobs, Islamic religious education and recognition of Muslim communities as full citizens, within the democratic order. Its base is educated Muslims and zongo leaders. Its leverage lies in its schools and in the votes of Muslim communities across the country.

13.name: Presidential Commission
13.text:
When the National Liberation Council handed power to civilians in 1969, it left behind a three-man Presidential Commission to act as head of state: Brigadier Akwasi Afrifa, Major-General Albert Kwesi Ocran and police chief John Harlley. On 1 January 1970 it still holds the presidency until a permanent president is chosen.

The commissioners see themselves as guarantors of the constitution rather than partisans, protecting order, the armed forces and the settlement of 1966. They are pro-Western but stress national unity. Their leverage lies in their formal powers and in the respect they command in the barracks.

14.name: National House of Chiefs
14.text:
The National House of Chiefs brings together paramount chiefs from all regions to advise on customary law and chieftaincy affairs, and the 1969 constitution strengthens its role. Many chiefs who suffered under Nkrumah's interference have welcomed the Second Republic.

The chiefs defend stool lands, customary authority and their role in local government, and favour a cautious, conservative course with little interest in the Cold War. Their base is rural Ghana, where chiefs still allocate land and settle disputes. Their leverage lies in their influence over cocoa-growing communities and in their sway over voters.

15.name: Association of Ghana Industries
15.text:
The Association of Ghana Industries represents the country's manufacturers, from foreign subsidiaries in Tema to Ghanaian firms that grew under Nkrumah's import substitution. Since 1966 it has lobbied for the sale of state enterprises and for privileged access to import licences and foreign exchange.

The AGI wants protection for local industry, cheaper credit and the transfer of loss-making state firms to private owners, while warning against sharp devaluation. Its members are factory owners and managers. Its leverage lies in jobs and investment, which the government needs to deliver on its promises of growth.

16.name: United Nationalist Party
16.text:
The United Nationalist Party was formed in 1969 around the Kumasi lawyer Joe Appiah, a former Nkrumah associate turned opponent, and won only two seats in the elections. It survives on 1 January 1970 as a small opposition party in Parliament.

The UNP favours free enterprise, limited government, individual liberties and strong guarantees for property and the courts, and criticises both Busia's heavy-handedness and Nkrumahist statism. It is pro-Western. Its base is Ashanti professionals and businessmen. Its leverage lies in Appiah's personal reputation and in its ability to tip close votes.

17.name: Guardians of the Volta
17.text:
The Akosombo Dam flooded some 740 towns and villages when the Volta Lake filled in the 1960s, displacing around 80,000 people into hastily built resettlement townships. Teachers, chiefs and agricultural officers among the resettled communities now speak out for the people and land lost under the water.

They demand fair compensation, fertile farmland, protection of the lakeshore and controls on the waterborne diseases spreading along it. They also warn against deforestation in the cocoa belt. Their base is the resettlement towns of the Volta basin. Their leverage lies in the moral weight of the displaced and the national symbolism of the dam.

18.name: All People's Republican Party
18.text:
The All People's Republican Party was founded in 1969 by P.K.K. Quaidoo, a former CPP minister who broke with Nkrumah in the early 1960s. It won no seats in the August elections but remains active as a voice for moderate former Nkrumahists.

The APRP favours a mixed economy with a strong state role, welfare and education, Pan-African solidarity and non-alignment rather than Busia's open Western orientation. Its base is former CPP voters in the Central and Western regions who cannot support the banned party. Its leverage lies in its potential to gather the Nkrumahist vote legally.

19.name: Ghana Young Pioneers
19.text:
The Ghana Young Pioneers were Nkrumah's youth movement, founded in 1960 to raise a new generation in the spirit of African socialism and loyalty to the Osagyefo. The movement was dissolved after the 1966 coup, but many former Pioneer leaders and members stay in touch.

They hold to Nkrumah's independent scientific socialism, Pan-Africanism and non-alignment, admiring China and Yugoslavia as much as the Soviet Union. Their base is young men and women who grew up under Nkrumah, now in schools and workplaces. Their leverage lies in a disciplined network that could be revived quickly.

20.name: People's Action Party
20.text:
The People's Action Party was founded in 1969 by Imoru Ayarna and won two seats in the August elections, mainly in the Northern Region. It is a small opposition party on 1 January 1970.

The PAP campaigns on the neglect of the north, demands roads, schools and jobs for northern communities and plays on resentment of the southern elites who dominate the state. It also calls for Ghanaians to be first in employment and trade. Its base is northern voters and migrants in the southern towns. Its leverage lies in regional grievance, which grows with every budget that passes the north by.

21.name: Action Groupers
21.text:
The Action Groupers were the militant youth arm of the National Liberation Movement, the Ashanti nationalist party that fought the CPP with bombs and street violence in the 1950s. Its veterans in Kumasi still remember their war against Nkrumah's followers.

They glorify Asante power, demand a hard line against Nkrumahists, communists and aliens, and admire military strongmen. Their numbers are small but they have experience in organised violence. Their base is Kumasi youth and old NLM militants. Their leverage lies in intimidation and in their links to Ashanti patrons.

22.name: Ghana Armed Forces
22.text:
The Ghana Armed Forces overthrew Nkrumah in 1966 and ruled through the National Liberation Council until October 1969. Back in the barracks, the army remains the country's strongest institution, and ambitious officers such as Lieutenant-Colonel Ignatius Kutu Acheampong watch the civilian government closely.

The officers are mostly pro-Western and anti-communist, but resent budget cuts, the loss of privileges and the meddling of politicians. Their base is the barracks of Accra, Kumasi and Tamale. Their leverage is the precedent of 1966: a coup is the one way to change the government without an election.

23.name: Asanteman
23.text:
The Ashanti Kingdom, Asanteman, is ruled from Manhyia Palace in Kumasi by the Asantehene, Otumfuo Sir Osei Agyeman Prempeh II, enthroned in 1931 and now elderly. The Golden Stool remains the symbol of the Asante nation, and the kingdom's chiefs are among the most powerful in Ghana.

The Asantehene's court defends Asante land, culture and authority, backs the Progress Party and the end of Nkrumah's interference in chieftaincy, and favours a federal or at least decentralised Ghana. Its base is the Ashanti and Brong-Ahafo regions. Its leverage lies in the loyalty of millions of Asante.
